source.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
source.authors: R. Fear; Payel Mukhopadhyay; Michael McCabe; Alberto Bietti; Miles Cranmer

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses difference-of-means concept directions and activation steering, inspired in part by work on refusal directions, to control physical phenomena in a physics model. It reports those steering results, but does not test refusal behavior or any other behavior named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study is about Walrus, a physics foundation model, and physical concepts such as vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed—not safety-trained chat models or refusal. Its physical steering results are recorded under fits_no_version; cited results about refusal are not recorded as this study's own results.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the difference-in-means direction method from the original refusal paper and applies it to Walrus, a physics simulation model. It steers physical concepts (vorticity, diffusion, simulation speed). It reports no refusal measure, no chat or safety-trained model and no harmful/harmless contrast, so its results bear on no claim version. The method serves as a tool, and only its steering performance in a new domain is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that difference-of-means directions give causal control over vorticity, diffusion and simulation speed in Walrus. They say these directions appear domain-general across physical systems, which they take as early evidence for linear, abstract physical representations.
record.recipe_differences: It adapts difference-of-mean activation directions and causal activation intervention, but applies them to physical simulation features in Walrus rather than harmful-versus-harmless instructions and refusal. The paper normalizes activations by position and injects a scaled direction across tokens and time steps, followed by renormalization.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that retaining versus averaging spatial dimensions changes outcomes: spatially averaged directions tend to produce more interpretable and physically consistent, more linear-looking steering; directions with spatial structure can produce more extreme but less natural results and mirrored changes. The initial simulation's distance from the target regime also affects the steering strength needed and whether resulting fields remain physically plausible.

fits_no_version.finding: Difference-of-means directions from contrasting physical regimes, injected at block 39 of Walrus, suppress or induce vortices, increase or decrease diffusion, and speed up or slow down simulated dynamics. Evidence is qualitative and visual only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a physics foundation model, difference-of-means directions for physical features causally steer the corresponding simulated phenomena when added or subtracted at inference.

fits_no_version.finding: Shear Flow-derived vorticity and speed directions produce analogous effects in Rayleigh-Bénard, Euler Quadrant and Gray-Scott systems. Bidirectionality depends on spatial averaging versus retaining spatial structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Physical concept directions transfer across some simulation domains, with linear bidirectional behaviour mainly when spatially averaged.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-domain vorticity steering with spatial structure retained yields mirrored (inverted) field changes under negative steering. Spatially averaged directions give a more linear, natural-looking response.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retaining spatial structure in a steering tensor changes the linearity and physical plausibility of concept steering.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025), as stated in the paper; venue metadata supplied as arXiv.org
record.problems: The reported steering outcomes are primarily qualitative and visual, without numerical behavioral metrics or uncertainty estimates. The authors identify physical plausibility of steered outputs as an open problem, note that spatially retained directions can produce unrealistic field changes, and say high steering strength can distort fields. The study focuses on Walrus block 39 and does not report a layer sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified results were stated. Redundant field-by-field visualizations in Appendix Figures 7–9 were summarized in the relevant row notes rather than entered as separate rows when they described the same steering condition and physical effect.

untested.parts: No refusal direction, no ablation or addition affecting refusal, no capability check on a language model.
No weight-edit or abliteration of released chat models.
No affine, cone or multi-direction account of refusal; spatial versus averaged physics directions are not a refusal-geometry test.
Transfer is between physical simulation systems, not languages, model variants or base/instruct models.

record.verdict_notes: The original refusal paper is cited only as methodological inspiration. All results are qualitative, with no metrics, uncertainty or layer sweep (block 39 only). Relation could arguably be cites_only/T6, but the method is used directly as a tool, so T4 is kept.

versions.untested_parts: No refusal direction, refusal ablation or addition, or general chat capability was tested.
No weight-edit or abliteration test in released chat models.
No jailbreak suppression of a refusal direction or robustness training against such ablation.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No harmfulness judgment or refusal-decision representation was tested.
Transfer is tested between physical systems, not languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
No refusal training regimen or training-stage comparison.
No reasoning chat model or refusal behavior tested.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the shear-flow vortex direction to suppress vortices.
rows.measure: Visible vortex suppression in the output flow.
rows.value: Figure shows negative-injection output; text describes progressive vortex suppression as α increases.
rows.note: The paper does not quantify this physical outcome; the text describes the overall suppression trend.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the shear-flow vortex direction to suppress vortices.
rows.measure: Visible vortex suppression in the output flow.
rows.value: Figure shows negative-injection output; text describes progressive vortex suppression as α increases.
rows.note: The text says the flow becomes smooth and parallel, characteristic of a laminar regime, as suppression increases.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the shear-flow vortex direction to suppress vortices.
rows.measure: Visible vortex suppression in the output flow.
rows.value: Figure shows negative-injection output; text describes progressive vortex suppression as α increases.
rows.note: The text describes the overall intervention as transforming the flow toward a laminar regime.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Positive injection of the shear-flow vortex direction into laminar-regime simulations.
rows.measure: Induction of vortical structures in the output flow.
rows.value: Figure shows positive-injection output; text says small injections produce subtle perturbations and incipient rotation.
rows.note: The result is a physical-flow outcome, not a refusal measure.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Positive injection of the shear-flow vortex direction into laminar-regime simulations.
rows.measure: Induction of vortical structures in the output flow.
rows.value: Figure shows positive-injection output; text says small injections produce subtle perturbations and incipient rotation.
rows.note: The text reports the effect scales with steering strength.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Positive injection of the shear-flow vortex direction into laminar-regime simulations.
rows.measure: Induction and development of vortical structures in the output flow.
rows.value: Figure shows injected vortices; text says moderate injections (α ≈ 0.4 to 0.5) yield well-formed vortices.
rows.note: The paper describes well-formed vortex induction for the stated moderate-strength range.
rows.check: numbers_found '2/2' has no meaning here: the paper gives no numeric outcome, only a qualitative description over the α≈0.4–0.5 range. Figure 3 shows α up to 0.4 only.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Positive injection of the shear-flow diffusion direction.

conditions.value: Shear Flow vortex regime; figure datafile shear_flow_Reynolds_5e4_Schmidt_2e-1

rows.measure: Appearance of the fluid interface and related physical fields.
rows.value: More diffuse-looking interface; appendix describes larger, more spread-out pressure minima and y-velocity zones, and smoother x-velocity gradients.
rows.locator: §3.3.1, Figure 4; Appendix A.2, Figure 9; Appendix B.1 Table 1
rows.note: The paper describes these changes as consistent with increasing diffusion.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection (subtraction) of the shear-flow diffusion direction.

conditions.value: Shear Flow vortex regime; figure datafile shear_flow_Reynolds_5e4_Schmidt_2e-1

rows.measure: Appearance of the fluid interface and related physical fields.
rows.value: Sharper interface; appendix describes reduced size of the corresponding pressure and y-velocity regions and sharper x-velocity gradients.
rows.locator: §3.3.1, Figure 4; Appendix A.2, Figure 9; Appendix B.1 Table 1
rows.note: The paper describes these changes as consistent with decreasing diffusion.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Positive injection of the shear-flow speed direction derived from different frame rates.

conditions.value: Shear Flow vortex regime; figure datafile shear_flow_Reynolds_5e4_Schmidt_5e-1

rows.measure: Timing of vortex development during rollout.
rows.value: Vortex forms earlier and is larger and more developed at the displayed frame.
rows.note: The figure caption identifies the right-hand images as α = 0.1, 0, and -0.1.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection (subtraction) of the shear-flow speed direction.

conditions.value: Shear Flow vortex regime; figure datafile shear_flow_Reynolds_5e4_Schmidt_5e-1

rows.measure: Timing of vortex development during rollout.
rows.value: Vortex formation is delayed; it has barely formed at the displayed frame compared with the unmodified simulation.
rows.note: The paper describes the positive and negative interventions as speeding and delaying development, respectively.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Transfer of the Shear Flow vortex direction to Rayleigh-Bénard Convection, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Convection patterns and secondary pressure-field changes.
rows.value: Convection patterns appear earlier and are larger with positive steering; pressure field also changes substantially.
rows.note: The paper reports a positive-direction increase in convection for spatially averaged transfer.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the Shear Flow vortex direction into Rayleigh-Bénard Convection, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Convection patterns and secondary pressure-field changes.
rows.value: Convection decreases with negative steering; pressure field also changes substantially.
rows.note: The paper reports the opposite convection trend for negative spatially averaged steering.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Transfer of the Shear Flow vortex direction to Rayleigh-Bénard Convection with spatial dimensions retained.

conditions.value: Shear Flow-derived vorticity; spatial dimensions retained

rows.measure: Convection patterns and pressure-field changes.
rows.value: Convection increases, with large high- and low-pressure zones.
rows.note: The paper says the simple positive-increase/negative-decrease relationship disappears when spatial dimensions are retained.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the Shear Flow vortex direction into Rayleigh-Bénard Convection with spatial dimensions retained.

conditions.value: Shear Flow-derived vorticity; spatial dimensions retained

rows.measure: Convection patterns and pressure-field changes.
rows.value: Convection also increases, with large high- and low-pressure zones inverted relative to positive steering.
rows.note: Negative steering does not produce the expected decrease in convection under this transfer condition.
rows.check: Negative steering with spatial dimensions retained increased convection, opposite to the expected decrease. Relative to the row's own expected effect this is reversed rather than partial. It still bears on no claim version.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Transfer of the Shear Flow vortex direction to Euler Quadrant simulations, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Number and size of rotational flow features.
rows.value: Rotational features increase in size and number, especially at shock interfaces.
rows.note: The authors describe the rotational features as appearing at physically expected shock interfaces.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the Shear Flow vortex direction into Euler Quadrant simulations, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Number and size of rotational flow features.
rows.value: Rotational features decrease in size and number.
rows.note: This is a cross-system physical steering result, not a refusal result.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Transfer of the Shear Flow speed direction to Euler Quadrant simulations, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Position of shock fronts during rollout.
rows.value: Shock fronts move faster; the vertical shock line is farther along than in the unmodified image.
rows.note: The paper also notes rotational features along the shock front in this condition.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative injection of the Shear Flow speed direction into Euler Quadrant simulations, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Position of shock fronts during rollout.
rows.value: Shock fronts move slower; the vertical shock line is behind the unmodified image.
rows.note: The text compares the positive, unmodified, and negative shock-front positions.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Transfer of the Shear Flow vortex direction to Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion simulations, spatially averaged across positions.
rows.measure: Patterns in chemical concentration fields.
rows.value: Gliders transform into spiral patterns.
rows.note: The authors call this surprising because fluid vortices are not defined in this chemical system.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Vorticity steering in laminar Shear Flow with spatial dimensions retained.
rows.measure: Tracer, pressure, and velocity fields.
rows.value: Positive steering produces a smaller, less well-formed vortex in the tracer field and coordinated pressure and y-velocity changes.
rows.note: The paper says positive and negative steering produce opposite changes in pressure and y velocity, but the negative result is not a simple vorticity decrease.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative vorticity steering in laminar Shear Flow with spatial dimensions retained.
rows.measure: Tracer, pressure, and velocity fields.
rows.value: Pressure-field inversion rather than the flattening expected if vorticity were simply reduced.
rows.note: The authors explicitly say this negative result does not fit a linear increase/decrease interpretation.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Vorticity steering in laminar Shear Flow without spatial dimensions in the steering direction.
rows.measure: Tracer and secondary physical fields.
rows.value: A smaller, less well-formed vortex than with spatial dimensions retained, despite higher α; secondary-field changes are more subtle.
rows.note: The paper describes the spatially averaged result as more consistent with a linear steering response.

rows.subject: Walrus
rows.operation_detail: Negative vorticity steering in laminar Shear Flow without spatial dimensions in the steering direction.
rows.measure: Tracer and secondary physical fields.
rows.value: More natural-looking laminar flow; negative-direction secondary-field inversion is no longer present.
rows.note: The authors contrast this with the less natural-looking negative result when spatial dimensions are retained.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
